items.content:
OpenAI is proposing to remove access to its models in Cursor on November 12. 

OpenAI, Cursor CEO, and Anthropic founder all weighed in on X with so much subtly, I had to go Nancy Drew mode and dissect each tweet. 

My translation of each one 👇 

OpenAI - they trust the Cursor team, they don’t trust SpaceX, it’s a “proposal” so maybe this public tweet is a way to gain leverage in the negotiation (note that it came from the company account on a Friday night)

Cursor - seems surprised about the OpenAI tweet, sounds like they want to fight it, goes out of their way to say OpenAI is a small percent of traffic, calls into question their neutrality (though I don’t think the labs call themselves neutral) (and note it came from the CEO, not the company account)

Anthropic - reaffirms the trust in Cursor and reminds us that it’s been years of trust, highlights they’re providing more of the most constrained carrot (compute), takes positive spin on the acquisition by SpaceX (note that it came from founder Tom who we don’t hear from often and not Anthropic account, and note that Cursor CEO reshared) 

Do I think it’ll hold? It’s hard for me to see a world where OpenAI continues to provide model access to a Musk-led company. Maybe if the structure of SpaceX shifts to allow for it, but that’s a big shift. 

Do I think Anthropic got a big PR boost? No, devs are focused on the loss of O, not the maintenance of partnership with A. They care about their own work. 

What’s the theme here? TRUST. How long has the trust been there, who holds the relationship, what hurt it, how to keep it. At the end of the day, all of these companies are led by people.

Most people haven’t updated their priors yet, but over the long run, safety challenges are exactly the same for open-source and closed-source models.

You need to align models at a fundamental behavioral level and ensure that this alignment is robust, comprehensive, and core to the model’s behavior.

In the long term, no amount of sandboxing, guardrailing, manifold-limited alignment, or cherry-on-top training will buy you cheap safety.

If space, time, particles, and physical fields emerged with the early universe, did mathematical structure emerge too?

Or could abstract relations—symmetry, groups, transformations, geometry, and logical consistency—be conceptually prior to physical spacetime?

That same mathematical language reaches directly into AI. Gaussian Process (GP) is a machine learning models built from functions, kernels, covariance structures, and linear algebra, another example of abstract mathematics becoming a predictive model of observed physical reality.

Linear Algebra and Optimization for Machine Learning [516-page textbook]: https://t.co/s6oCEvVMKS
—
This textbook is organized around its 2 main themes:
[Amazon Summary]

1. Linear algebra and its applications: The chapters focus on the basics of linear algebra together with their common applications to singular value decomposition, matrix factorization, similarity matrices (kernel methods), and graph analysis. Numerous machine learning applications have been used as examples, such as spectral clustering, kernel-based classification, and outlier detection. The tight integration of linear algebra methods with examples from machine learning differentiates this book from generic volumes on linear algebra. The focus is clearly on the most relevant aspects of linear algebra for machine learning and to teach readers how to apply these concepts.

2. Optimization and its applications: Much of machine learning is posed as an optimization problem in which we try to maximize the accuracy of regression and classification models. The “parent problem” of optimization-centric machine learning is least-squares regression. Interestingly, this problem arises in both linear algebra and optimization, and is one of the key connecting problems of the two fields. Least-squares regression is also the starting point for support vector machines, logistic regression, and recommender systems. Furthermore, the methods for dimensionality reduction and matrix factorization also require the development of optimization methods. A general view of optimization in computational graphs is discussed together with its applications to back propagation in neural networks.

items.content:
Still expecting the CIO to say “mea culpa” when resilience fails?

You may have once.

Today, digital resilience is a board responsibility because disruption reaches operations and business continuity, far beyond the data center and IT function alone.

Microblog  by  @antgrasso 

Why has the responsibility moved?

Because a digital failure rarely stays inside IT.

If a cloud outage stops online orders, restoring the infrastructure is a technology problem. Deciding which business services must return first is an executive leadership decision.

If a cyberattack forces a factory to slow production, the CIO can coordinate recovery of the systems. But who decides how long operations can tolerate the disruption? Who decides what customers should be told and which business risks are acceptable?

Executive leadership needs to make those decisions.

Digital resilience now depends on knowing which operations the company cannot afford to lose and making sure technology recovery supports them. The CIO remains central, but cannot carry that responsibility alone.

And resilience starts before the incident.

Investment choices and continuity plans need agreement while everything is still working. Accountability must already be clear.

When disruption arrives, the CIO can restore technology. Executive leadership must already know how the business will continue.

I met a few Chilean founders this week and have been telling them the same story.

Chile is a long, ...
items.content:
I met a few Chilean founders this week and have been telling them the same story.

Chile is a long, thin country, ~2,500 miles from north to south, and so narrow that we don't even have a concept of east or west. Just north, center, and south. Every time I come here, I try to spend at least one or two days in the very south, in Patagonia. If you've ever been there, you know it's far from everywhere, pretty much the end of the map.

Many years ago, I met a woman there who had lived her whole life in a small city in the south. She told me she was going to the north of Chile to visit a doctor. I was so confused. Why travel thousands of miles when the big cities of the center were closer? Then I understood: her "north" was a town a few hours up the road. Anything beyond it was unimaginable. Her north was my very south.

When you start a company, you need to set a north. How far you imagine you want to go. But every north is arbitrary, and every north is someone else's south. If north is your ambition, you need to remove the idea that there is a north in the first place.
